# Video-Language Models for Understanding

Given a clip $\mathbf{V} = (\mathbf{I}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{I}_T) \in \mathbb{R}^{T \times H \times W \times 3}$, video understanding asks *what is happening, where, when, and who is doing it?* Two model families dominate the 2024–2026 landscape:

1. **Autoregressive vision-language models (VLMs)**: a vision encoder lifts each frame to tokens, a *projector* compresses them, and an autoregressive LLM decoder *generates* a textual answer — caption, label, or free-form response. The Qwen-VL series (Qwen-VL [@bai2023qwenvl] → Qwen2-VL [@wang2024qwen2vl] → Qwen2.5-VL [@bai2025qwen25vl] → Qwen3-VL [@team2025qwen3vl]), LLaVA-OneVision [@li2024llavaonevision], InternVL3 [@chen2024internvl], and Molmo [@deitke2024molmo] are the reference families.
2. **Representation-style video encoders**: a network maps a clip to a single embedding (or a small set of pooled tokens), scored against a label or contrasted against text embeddings. VideoMAEv2 [@wang2023videomaev2], V-JEPA 2 [@assran2025vjepa2], and InternVideo2 [@wang2024internvideo2] are the modern reference encoders — the architectural successors to the C3D/SlowFast/ViViT/VideoMAE line covered in the previous chapter.

The two families are not disjoint: representation models are often the *vision tower* inside an autoregressive VLM, and an autoregressive VLM can be turned into a representation model by pooling its vision tokens and training a contrastive head — the recipe used by the Janus family [@chen2025januspro] of *dual* understanding+generation models (@sec-vlm-specialised).

This chapter covers four things: the downstream tasks (@sec-video-tasks), the architectural design choices that distinguish video VLMs (@sec-video-vlms-arch), the two-stage retrieval+reranking pipeline used in production video search (@sec-video-retrieval), and a condensed benchmark map (@sec-video-benchmarks-short).

## Notation {#sec-video-notation}

| Concept | Notation | Definition |
|:--------|:---------|:-----------|
| **Clip** | $\mathbf{V} \in \mathbb{R}^{T \times H \times W \times 3}$ | $T$ frames sampled from a longer video. |
| **Native FPS** | $f_{\text{src}}$ | Frame rate of the source file (24–30 fps). |
| **Sample FPS** | $f_{\text{s}}$ | Frame rate the model consumes (1–8 fps for VLMs, 8–32 fps for action encoders). |
| **Frame budget** | $T$ | Frames per clip, bounded by GPU memory and context length. |
| **Vision token** | $\mathbf{z}_i \in \mathbb{R}^d$ | Embedding emitted by the vision encoder, fed to the decoder. |
| **Token budget** | $N_v$ | Vision tokens after compression; directly costs decoder context. |
| **Temporal certificate** | $\tau_c$ | Minimum duration a human needs to watch to verify an annotation [@mangalam2023egoschema]. Larger $\tau_c$ ⇒ longer-range reasoning required. |

: Video-language model terminology. {#tbl-video-repr}

**Two invariants worth fixing up front**: (1) Sample FPS is almost always far below native FPS — a 30-fps, 10-minute video has 18,000 frames, so even at 1–2 fps a clip is 600–1,200 frames, still aggressively pooled before the decoder. (2) Temporal compression (sample FPS, frame selection) and spatial compression (tokens per frame) are tuned **independently** and trade off differently per task (@sec-token-budgets).

## Downstream Video Tasks {#sec-video-tasks}

@tbl-video-tasks summarizes the downstream tasks that recur throughout this chapter and the benchmark survey (@sec-video-benchmarks-short).

| Task | Formulation | Metric |
|:-----|:------------|:-------|
| **Action recognition** | Clip $\to$ class $c^* \in \mathcal{C}$ (or multi-label $\hat{\mathbf{y}} \in \{0,1\}^{|\mathcal{C}|}$) | Top-1/5 accuracy; mAP for multi-label |
| **Temporal action localization (TAL)** | Long video $\to$ set of $(t_s, t_e, c)$ triples | mAP@$\tau$, see @eq-map-tau |
| **Spatio-temporal action detection** | Per-frame bounding box + action label | Frame-level mAP @ spatial IoU 0.5 |
| **Video captioning** | Clip $\to$ natural-language description (or a timestamped sequence for *dense* captioning) | BLEU/METEOR/CIDEr/SPICE; SODA$_c$ [@fujita2020soda] for dense |
| **Video question answering** | (Clip, question) $\to$ answer — multiple-choice, open-ended, or *grounded* (answer + supporting segment) | MCQ accuracy; LLM-judge for open-ended; IoU for grounded |
| **Temporal grounding / moment retrieval** | (Video, text query) $\to$ segment $(t_s, t_e)$, or corpus-scale (video, moment) pair (VCMR) | Recall@N, IoU=$\tau$, see @eq-moment-r |
| **Video retrieval** | Rank a corpus by similarity to a text/video query | Recall@\{1,5,10\}, median rank |
| **Tracking (SOT / MOT)** | Bounding box per frame, with identity persistence for MOT | AUC (SOT); HOTA [@luiten2021hota] (MOT) |
| **Video object segmentation (VOS)** | Pixel mask per frame, optionally from a referring phrase | $\mathcal{J}\&\mathcal{F}$ |
| **Long-video understanding** | Narrative reasoning, memory, aggregation over $\geq 5$ min clips | MCQ accuracy (LongVideoBench, MLVU, EgoSchema) |
| **Egocentric understanding** | Head-mounted-camera video; extreme motion, hands/objects in close view | Task-dependent (Ego4D suite) |

: Downstream video understanding tasks. {#tbl-video-tasks}

$$
\text{mAP}@\tau = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{C}|}\sum_{c \in \mathcal{C}} \text{AP}_c\bigl(\text{IoU} \geq \tau\bigr)
$$ {#eq-map-tau}

$$
\text{R@N, IoU}=\tau \;=\; \frac{1}{|Q|}\sum_{q \in Q} \mathbb{1}\!\left[\max_{i \leq N} \text{IoU}(\hat{m}_i^{(q)}, m^{(q)}) \geq \tau\right]
$$ {#eq-moment-r}

where $\hat{m}_i^{(q)}$ is the $i$-th predicted moment for query $q$ and $m^{(q)}$ the ground truth.

**Interview Insight**: In 2024–2026 papers, MCQ format (Video-MME, MVBench, NeXT-QA) has become the default VQA evaluation precisely because it is robust to free-form generation noise — it isolates *understanding* from *instruction-following* and *formatting*, which dominate open-ended scores.

## Architecture: From Q-Former to M-RoPE {#sec-video-vlms-arch}

Every model in this section shares a ViT-to-LLM template: a vision encoder lifts each frame to patch tokens, a *projector* compresses them, and an autoregressive LLM consumes the projected tokens interleaved with text. Three design choices distinguish video VLMs from image VLMs: **token compression**, **temporal positional encoding**, and **pretraining masking**.

### Token Compression {#sec-token-budgets}

A ViT at 384×384 with 14×14 patches emits $(384/14)^2 \approx 730$ tokens per frame. At 32 frames, that is $\sim$23K tokens — already saturating a 32K-context LLM with the vision side alone. Every video VLM applies a compression step between encoder and decoder:

| Family | Mechanism | Examples |
|:-------|:----------|:---------|
| **Q-Former / Perceiver Resampler** | $K$ learned query tokens cross-attend to frame tokens, producing exactly $K$ outputs. Cheap to learn but adds parameters; viewed as a bottleneck since 2024. | Video-LLaMA [@zhang2023videollama], VideoChat2 [@li2024mvbench] |
| **Pixel-shuffle / patch merging** | Parameter-free $r \times r$ spatial pooling reduces tokens by $r^2$, then a linear projection. The 2024–2026 default. | Qwen2-VL onwards: 2×2 merge $\Rightarrow$ ~4× fewer tokens for near-zero quality loss |
| **Slow-Fast / two-stream sampling** | A few "slow" frames at full resolution, the rest "fast" at aggressive spatial compression — decouples temporal density from spatial detail. | SlowFast [@feichtenhofer2019slowfast], Apollo [@zohar2024apollo] |
| **Learned temporal pooling** | A fixed small token budget per frame regardless of resolution, or KV-cache compression for very long clips. | LLaMA-VID [@li2024llamavid] (2 tokens/frame); Video-XL [@shu2024videoxl] |

: Token compression strategies for video VLMs. {#tbl-token-compression}

### Temporal Positional Encoding {#sec-temporal-pos}

The decoder needs to know *when* each vision token came from. Four approaches:

- **Interleaved time tokens**: a literal text token like `<frame_5>` or `t=12.3s` precedes each frame's visual tokens. Cheap and general, but eats context.
- **Multi-axis RoPE (M-RoPE)** (Qwen2-VL onwards): the standard 1D rotary embedding [@su2021roformer] is decomposed into three independent axes $(t, h, w)$, each rotating a third of the head dimensions:

$$
\text{M-RoPE}(\mathbf{x}; t, h, w) = \big[\,\text{RoPE}(\mathbf{x}_{1:d/3}; t),\ \text{RoPE}(\mathbf{x}_{d/3+1:2d/3}; h),\ \text{RoPE}(\mathbf{x}_{2d/3+1:d}; w)\,\big]
$$ {#eq-mrope}

  Qwen2.5-VL keys $t$ to **absolute time in seconds** (not frame index), enabling 10-hour clips at variable FPS. Qwen3-VL **interleaves** the three axes across head dimensions (rather than three contiguous blocks) for better long-context generalization, and adds explicit text-based `<time>` tokens so the model is trained to *cite* timestamps when grounding a claim.
- **TMRoPE** (Qwen2.5-Omni [@xu2025qwen25omni]): extends M-RoPE to *cross-modality* temporal alignment — audio frames (40 ms) and video frames (500 ms) share a unified position-ID timeline, essential for synchronous audio+video input.
- **Factorized space-time attention** (TimeSformer, ViViT, Chapter 10): the vision *encoder* alternates spatial/temporal attention so the decoder receives tokens that already encode time. More common inside encoder-only models than decoder VLMs.

### Pretraining Masking {#sec-masking}

Self-supervised video encoders rely on masked autoencoding, and the masking strategy is the main design knob:

- **Tube masking** (VideoMAE [@tong2022videomae], 90–95% ratio): the same spatial mask is repeated across all $T$ frames, preventing trivial copying from adjacent frames (Chapter 10).
- **Dual masking** (VideoMAEv2 [@wang2023videomaev2]): masks both encoder and decoder inputs, enabling 1B-parameter encoders.
- **Unmasked-teacher distillation** (UMT [@li2023umt]): mask the *student*, but regress against an *unmasked* CLIP teacher's tokens — combines MAE-style efficiency with CLIP-style alignment.
- **Latent-prediction masking** (V-JEPA / V-JEPA 2 [@bardes2024vjepa; @assran2025vjepa2]): predict *features* of masked regions, not pixels — avoids wasting capacity on high-frequency texture, and V-JEPA 2 adds action-conditioned world-model capabilities.

**Interview Insight**: Tube masking and latent-prediction masking solve the same redundancy problem differently. Tube masking keeps the pixel-reconstruction objective but removes the "copy from a neighboring frame" shortcut by masking consistently across time. Latent-prediction masking instead changes the *target* — predicting features rather than pixels means the model is never rewarded for reconstructing high-frequency texture, which is a weaker training signal for semantics anyway.

## Case Study: The Qwen-VL Evolution {#sec-vlm-qwen}

The Qwen-VL series is the cleanest lens on the 2023–2026 architectural arc: each release retired a design choice that the rest of the field then followed.

| Release | Date | Key break(s) |
|:--------|:-----|:-------------|
| **Qwen-VL** [@bai2023qwenvl] | Aug 2023 | Fixed 448×448 input; Q-Former-style adapter with 256 learned queries + 2D RoPE on the query side. The design later inherited (and abandoned) by Video-LLaMA, VideoChat2. |
| **Qwen2-VL** [@wang2024qwen2vl] | Sep 2024 | **Native dynamic resolution** + pixel-shuffle (2×2 patch merge); **M-RoPE** over $(t,h,w)$; video as a sequence of frames at 2 fps through a 3D conv (temporal kernel 2), unifying image and video as a pseudo-3D volume. |
| **Qwen2.5-VL** [@bai2025qwen25vl] | Feb 2025 | **Window attention** in the ViT (linear in pixel count, fixes the ~30s memory wall); **absolute time embeddings** on top of M-RoPE keyed to real seconds; new video-text pretraining corpus. |
| **Qwen2.5-Omni** [@xu2025qwen25omni] | Mar 2025 | Extends to audio I/O with a unified "Thinker" transformer + streaming "Talker" decoder; introduces **TMRoPE** for synchronized audio+video timelines. |
| **Qwen3-VL** [@team2025qwen3vl] | Nov 2025 | 256K native multimodal context; **interleaved M-RoPE**; explicit text-based `<time>` tokens; **DeepStack** (multi-layer ViT features injected into multiple LLM layers); square-root loss reweighting for text/multimodal balance. |

: The Qwen-VL evolution — each release's architectural break became a field-wide default within months. {#tbl-qwen-evolution}

InternVL [@chen2024internvl] (adaptive visual-token resolution), Pixtral, Idefics, and Gemma 3 followed a parallel but convergent path: SigLIP-style encoders + pixel-shuffle + M-RoPE-family positional encoding is now the dominant 2024–2026 template, and the OpenAI CLIP ViT-L encoder has largely been retired in favor of **SigLIP-SO400M**.

## Specialized Video VLMs {#sec-vlm-specialised}

Beyond the generalist families above, three specialized lines matter for interviews:

**Long-video specialists** trade short-clip quality for consuming hundreds-to-thousands of frames. Two camps disagree on the trade-off: *compress aggressively* (LongVU [@shen2024longvu] uses DINOv2 cross-frame similarity to collapse redundant frames to one token each; Video-XL [@shu2024videoxl] uses Visual Summarization Tokens for KV-cache compression) vs. *extend the language context first* (LongVA [@zhang2024longva] extends the LLM to 224K tokens, then attaches the vision encoder — long-video capability transfers from language context for free). Eagle 2.5 [@huang2025eagle25] adds **Automatic Degrade Sampling**, dynamically trading visual against textual tokens at inference to stay within budget. Apollo [@zohar2024apollo] is a design-space *study* rather than a model: its headline finding, **scaling consistency**, is that design choices validated at 1.5B transfer almost perfectly to 7B — small-model ablations are trustworthy.

**Moment-localization specialists** treat $(t_s, t_e)$ prediction as a first-class output. LLaVA-MR [@lu2024llavamr] interleaves explicit time tokens with frame tokens (`<t=0.5> <frame_0> <t=1.0> <frame_1>...`) and applies a learned key-frame selector to allocate token budget unevenly. NumPro [@wu2024numpro] takes the opposite, much simpler approach: *overlay the frame index as a visible number on each frame* and let an off-the-shelf VLM read it — competitive zero-shot grounding with no temporal architecture at all, showing that explicit *visual* temporal cues can rival dense temporal embeddings.

**Dual understanding+generation models** unify perception and generation in one autoregressive loop. Janus-Pro [@chen2025januspro] **decouples the visual pathways**: a SigLIP encoder for understanding (semantics) and a VQ-tokenizer [@sun2024llamagen] for generation (discrete pixel tokens), sharing one transformer that predicts either text or image tokens depending on the task. The argument is that understanding wants high-level semantics while generation wants pixel-level detail — one encoder for both is a forced compromise. LlamaGen [@sun2024llamagen] is the underlying VQ tokenizer, demonstrating that next-token prediction over a well-trained codebook can match diffusion image quality (discussed further in the Video Generation chapter).

---

## Encoder-Only and Contrastive Video Models {#sec-vlm-encoder}

The pre-LLM line of Chapter 10 (C3D, I3D, SlowFast, TimeSformer, ViViT, VideoMAE) remains alive as the *vision tower* inside VLMs and for pure representation learning. The modern successors:

- **VideoMAEv2** [@wang2023videomaev2], **V-JEPA 2** [@assran2025vjepa2], **VideoMamba** [@li2024videomamba] (bidirectional state-space alternative to ViT, linear in frame count) deliver state-of-the-art *frozen-probe* accuracy on K400/SSv2 but are rarely deployed standalone — they sit inside VLMs (e.g., Apollo uses InternVideo2 as a second encoder).
- **InternVideo2** [@wang2024internvideo2] (successor to InternVideo [@wang2022internvideo]) trains in three stages — masked pretraining → cross-modal contrastive → supervised — on 6M+ hours, and is the reference video-native encoder of 2024–2026.

For **retrieval**, almost all contrastive video-text models follow the CLIP4Clip [@luo2022clip4clip] template: take a pretrained image-text CLIP, encode $T$ sampled frames independently, then **mean-pool** over time — mean pooling beat transformers and LSTMs in the original ablation and the result has held up. Modern variants: **ViCLIP** [@wang2024internvid], trained on InternVid-10M-FLT (the post-WebVid replacement corpus); **LanguageBind-Video** [@zhu2024languagebind], which binds video/audio/depth/thermal to a shared language embedding space via an OpenCLIP anchor; and InternVideo2 in its contrastive mode, which beats ViCLIP on most 2025–2026 leaderboards.

---

## Video Retrieval and the Two-Stage Pipeline {#sec-video-retrieval}

Production text-to-video search (clip databases, RAG over video corpora) converges on the same two-stage pattern as dense-retrieval-plus-cross-encoder in NLP:

1. **First stage — fast retrieval**: a bi-encoder embeds queries and video segments into a shared space; top-$K$ candidates come from an ANN index over cosine similarity. Must scan millions of clips quickly.
2. **Second stage — reranker**: a cross-modal scorer re-orders the top-$K$ candidates using cross-attention between query and candidate. Slow per item, but runs on only a few hundred candidates.

The split exists because first-stage embeddings lose cross-modal interactions that make rerankers expressive, while rerankers are too slow to run on the full corpus.

**Pre-LLM pipelines** trained frame-level (CLIP4Clip) or clip-level (I3D, ViViT) encoders with InfoNCE on text-video corpora (HowTo100M [@miech2019howto100m], WebVid [@bain2021frozen]). **Modern pipelines** instead adapt a generative VLM into a representation model: continue training with a bidirectional (non-causal) attention mask, pool token outputs into a single embedding, then fine-tune with InfoNCE on (query, relevant, irrelevant) triples — the same recipe that turned LLaMA-2 into E5-Mistral for text retrieval, applied to video.

**Rerankers** fall into three categories. Cross-encoder rerankers run a multimodal transformer over (query, candidate) jointly and produce a scalar score, trained with a margin/pairwise loss:

$$
\mathcal{L} = \max\bigl(0,\, m - s(q, d^{+}) + s(q, d^{-})\bigr)
$$ {#eq-rerank-margin}

on (positive, hard-negative) pairs from the first stage (CrossTVR [@li2024crosstvr]). **LLM-as-reranker** approaches (UniME-V2 [@gu2025unimev2]) pass the query and candidate to an instruction-tuned MLLM and score the log-probability of "relevant" — strong but expensive, often distilled into a smaller dedicated reranker for production.

The big *training* corpora for retrieval — HowTo100M (136M ASR-aligned clips, noisy by design), WebVid-10M (10M stock-footage clips, **taken down in late 2024** over a copyright dispute), InternVid (7M videos, 234M LLM-recaptioned sentences, the post-WebVid standard), and Panda-70M [@chen2024panda70m] (70M auto-captioned, the largest open corpus) — have no canonical test split; they are training-only.

|:------------|:----------------------|:------------------|:------|

| Action recognition (motion) | SSv2 [@goyal2017ssv2] | — | Different label per motion direction — separates real video models from frame-bag classifiers |
| Spatio-temporal detection | AVA [@gu2018ava] | — | Non-saturated; benchmark of choice for SlowFast/MViTv2 |
| Short-clip MCQ VQA | **MVBench** [@li2024mvbench] + Perception Test [@patraucean2023perceptiontest] | NeXT-QA [@xiao2021nextqa] | MVBench is the de-facto 2024–2026 short-clip number |

| Long-video MCQ VQA | **LongVideoBench** [@wu2024longvideobench] + MLVU [@zhou2024mlvu] | LVBench, HourVideo | Standard long-video trio: LVB + Video-MME-long + MLVU |
| "True temporal" MCQ VQA | TempCompass [@liu2024tempcompass] / TVBench [@cores2024tvbench] | — | Paired-clip tests; most 2023–2024 models score near chance |

| Captioning + retrieval | MSR-VTT | VATEX, YouCook2 | MSR-VTT 1K-A is the long-running retrieval leaderboard |
| Egocentric | Ego4D + EPIC-Kitchens-100 + EgoSchema [@mangalam2023egoschema] | — | Canonical egocentric trio |
| Tracking | LaSOT/GOT-10k/TrackingNet (SOT); MOT17/20 + DanceTrack (MOT) | — | HOTA + AUC metrics |

: Default benchmarks per task family. {#tbl-video-bench}

**What a 2026 paper reports**: a generalist video VLM needs **MVBench + Video-MME + Perception Test** (short-clip core), **LongVideoBench + MLVU** (long-video core), and at least one of TVBench/TempCompass/Vinoground as a "true temporal" sanity check. A *contrastive* retrieval paper instead reports **MSR-VTT 1K-A + DiDeMo retrieval + K400 zero-shot + SSv2 linear probe** — the CLIP4Clip template, stable since 2021.

## Trends and Open Problems {#sec-video-open}

- **Q-Former is out, pixel-shuffle is in.** Every major 2024 family dropped Q-Former for a parameter-free spatial merger; it survives only in older lineages (Video-LLaMA, mPLUG-Owl3).
- **Temporal encoding consolidated on M-RoPE** (or near-variants like InternVL3's V2PE). Vision encoders converged on SigLIP-SO400M.
- **Data quality beat data scale.** The WebVid-10M takedown forced the field onto InternVid + ShareGPT4Video + LLaVA-Video-178K + Panda-70M, all LLM-recaptioned — the single biggest quality jump from 2024 to 2025.
- **Frame access $\ne$ temporal reasoning.** Early "temporal" benchmarks (NeXT-QA, MVBench) could be solved by accessing a few frames cleverly. The "true temporal" wave (TVBench, TempCompass, Vinoground) — where the answer requires *integrating* information across many ordered frames — showed most 2024 models at chance.
- **Long-video memory is unsolved even at 256K–1M token context.** Visual-Needle-In-A-Haystack probes show accuracy degrades sharply for evidence in the *middle* of long contexts; the two camps (extend context vs. compress aggressively) disagree on the trade-off.
- **The grounding gap.** NeXT-GQA measures the fraction of correct MCQ answers that are *also* correctly temporally grounded — as of 2026, even the strongest models are 20–30 points below their MCQ accuracy on this measure.
- **Evaluation methodology gaps**: MCQ leak (answer guessable from text alone — why TVBench exists), subtitle leak (Video-MME's with-subtitles split), and LLM-judge variance (MMBench-Video scores shift several points between GPT-4 and GPT-4o).
- **Cultural coverage**: most egocentric/instructional data is North American or European; a "general" video-understanding claim without multilingual/multi-cultural evaluation is incomplete.

---

## Interview Questions

**Q: Why is "token compression" necessary for video VLMs, and what are the main families?**

A ViT emits hundreds of tokens per frame; at even a few dozen frames this saturates an LLM's context budget before any text is added. The main families are: Q-Former/Perceiver-style learned queries (fixed output count, but adds trainable parameters and is viewed as a bottleneck); pixel-shuffle/patch-merging (parameter-free spatial pooling, the 2024–2026 default); slow-fast sampling (full resolution for a few "slow" frames, heavy compression for "fast" frames); and learned temporal pooling / KV-cache compression for very long clips. The trend has been away from learned-query bottlenecks toward parameter-free spatial compression plus smarter temporal sampling.

---

**Q: What problem does M-RoPE solve, and how did Qwen2.5-VL extend it for hour-long video?**

Standard 1D RoPE only encodes sequence position, but video tokens have three coordinates — time, row, column. M-RoPE decomposes the rotary embedding into three independent axes $(t, h, w)$, each rotating a third of the head dimensions, so the model natively understands frame ordering and spatial layout simultaneously. Qwen2-VL's $t$ axis was just the frame index, which breaks down for hour-long clips sampled at variable FPS. Qwen2.5-VL keys $t$ to **absolute time in seconds**, so a frame sampled at minute 47 carries that information regardless of how many frames were sampled before it — letting the model correctly ground claims like "this happened 47 minutes in" rather than "at frame 1411".

---

**Q: What is the "grounding gap," and why is it the most informative number for a long-video VLM?**

The grounding gap (measured by NeXT-GQA) is the difference between a model's MCQ accuracy and its accuracy when *also* required to predict the temporal segment that supports the answer. A model can get the right answer for the wrong reason — e.g., from language priors or a lucky frame — without actually "knowing when" the evidence occurred. As of 2026, even top models show a 20–30 point grounding gap, meaning a large fraction of "correct" answers are not actually temporally grounded. It's the single number that distinguishes genuine temporal understanding from pattern-matching.

---

**Q: Describe the two-stage retrieval-and-reranking pipeline for video search, and explain why it's split into two stages.**

Stage 1 is a bi-encoder: queries and video segments are embedded independently into a shared space, and an ANN index returns the top-$K$ candidates by cosine similarity — fast enough to scan millions of clips, but the embeddings can't capture fine-grained cross-modal interactions. Stage 2 is a reranker — a cross-attention model (or an LLM prompted to judge relevance) that scores the query jointly with each candidate, capturing interactions the first stage misses. It's too slow to run on the full corpus but cheap on the few hundred survivors of stage 1. This mirrors BM25-then-BERT-cross-encoder in text retrieval exactly.

---

**Q: Compare tube masking (VideoMAE) and latent-prediction masking (V-JEPA). Why do both approaches remain in use?**

Tube masking keeps a pixel-reconstruction objective but masks the *same spatial positions across all frames*, removing the shortcut of copying an unmasked neighbor in an adjacent frame — this forces the encoder to learn spatiotemporal structure while keeping a simple, well-understood loss. Latent-prediction masking (V-JEPA) instead changes the *target*: predict the *features* of masked regions in representation space, never rewarding the model for reconstructing high-frequency pixel texture. VideoMAE-style pretraining remains competitive and simple to implement; V-JEPA's approach yields representations that transfer better to downstream reasoning and supports action-conditioned world models (V-JEPA 2), at the cost of a more complex training setup (online target encoder, EMA updates).

---

**Q: Why did MVBench need to be replaced by TVBench and TempCompass for "true temporal" claims?**

MVBench (2024) was the first benchmark to construct 20 temporal-reasoning task types from existing clip sources, but many of its questions turned out to be answerable from a single frame or from world knowledge alone — a model could score well without actually integrating information across frames. TVBench filtered MVBench's source clips down to questions that genuinely require multi-frame reasoning, and most 2024 video LMs scored near chance on it at release. TempCompass goes further with *paired* clips that differ only in a temporal property (direction, speed, order) and an additional "paired accuracy" metric requiring the model to get *both* clips in a pair right — a much stricter test that exposes models relying on static-frame shortcuts.
